lessons.title: Worship & Prayer
lessons.description: Forms of worship, the role of prayer, and the significance of the Lord's Prayer.
lessons.content_html:
Why Do Christians Worship?

Worship is how Christians express their love and devotion to God. The word comes from the Old English ‘worthship’ — recognising that God is worthy of praise. Christians worship for many reasons: to thank God for creation and blessings, to ask for forgiveness, to seek guidance, and to strengthen their relationship with God. The Bible teaches, “Come, let us bow down in worship, let us kneel before the Lord our Maker” (Psalm 95:6).

Key Fact

Christians worship in four main ways — liturgical, non-liturgical, informal and private. Each serves the same purpose of honouring God but differs in structure and style.

Liturgical Worship

Liturgical worship follows the same set pattern every time. It is led by a priest or minister who guides the congregation through prayers, Bible readings, a sermon and symbolic actions such as the Eucharist. Roman Catholic, Orthodox and Anglican churches use liturgical worship.

Supporters value its familiarity — worshippers know what to expect. It connects Christians to centuries of tradition and provides the same structure in churches worldwide. The use of the Bible is central: readings follow a set lectionary so that all congregations hear the same passages on the same day.

Non-Liturgical Worship

Non-liturgical worship has no fixed order. Hymns, Bible readings and a sermon may be included, but the service is flexible and can change from week to week. It is commonly practised in Methodist, Baptist and United Reformed churches. The focus is on the word of God in the Bible, and services often respond directly to the needs of the congregation.

Informal worship includes charismatic worship, which is free-flowing and may include dance, clapping, calling out, speaking in tongues and modern music. Pentecostal and evangelical churches commonly practise this form. It is seen as more relevant to modern life and allows worshippers to express their faith spontaneously.

Quaker worship is another form of informal worship. There is no leader and no set structure. Worshippers sit in a circle in silent reflection and may speak when they feel moved by the Holy Spirit. This allows God to communicate directly with individuals.

Private Worship

Private worship is when a Christian praises God alone. It may include personal prayer, Bible reading, meditation, or using worship aids such as the rosary or icons. Jesus encouraged private worship: “When you pray, go into your room, close the door and pray to your Father, who is unseen” (Matthew 6:6). Private worship can use set prayers or the Christian’s own words.

Private worship gives Christians personal time with God away from the pressures of everyday life. Many believers set aside a regular time each day for personal devotion — reading a passage of Scripture, reflecting on its meaning and praying about their daily concerns. Some Christians use structured devotional guides, while others simply open the Bible and read. The advantage of private worship is that it allows a deeply personal relationship with God that communal services may not always provide.

Prayer

Prayer is communication with God. It can be silent or spoken, individual or communal. Christians pray for many reasons, remembered by the acronym STOP: Sorry (confession), Thank (gratitude), Others (intercession) and Please (petition). Jesus taught, “Whatever you ask for in prayer, believe that you have received it, and it will be yours” (Mark 11:24).

Set prayers are written down and used repeatedly by many Christians. They provide unity and tradition and are central to liturgical worship. An example is the Catholic grace before meals.

Informal prayer uses the Christian’s own words. It allows believers to express their personal emotions and concerns freely. Most Christians use informal prayers in private worship — these might be as simple as “Help me, God” or “Thank you, God.”

The Lord’s Prayer

When Jesus’s disciples asked how to pray, he taught them the Lord’s Prayer (Matthew 6:9–13). It is a model of good prayer because it combines praise of God with submission to His will, requests for daily needs, forgiveness and protection from evil.

“Our Father in heaven” — God is the Father of all people. “Hallowed be your name” — God’s name is holy and should be treated with reverence. “Your kingdom come, your will be done, on earth as it is in heaven” — Christians pray for God’s rule to be established. “Give us today our daily bread” — asking God to provide what is needed. “Forgive us our sins, as we forgive those who sin against us” — forgiveness must be both received and given. “Lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil” — asking for God’s protection.

Key Fact

The Lord’s Prayer teaches Christians that prayer should include praise (“hallowed be your name”), submission to God’s will, requests for daily needs, and forgiveness. It is said at worship, baptisms, marriages and funerals, uniting all Christian denominations.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For the 4-mark ‘Explain similarities and differences’ question, make sure your two examples are genuinely different — for example, contrast liturgical worship (set structure, Catholic Mass) with charismatic worship (free-flowing, Pentecostal). For 6-mark questions, you must refer to a source of Christian teaching such as Matthew 6:6 or the Lord’s Prayer. For 12-mark evaluations, always give arguments for and against, include specific Christian teachings, and reach a justified conclusion.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Christians worship in four main forms — liturgical (set structure), non-liturgical (flexible), informal/charismatic (free-flowing) and private (individual) — each serving the purpose of honouring God.
  • Prayer is communication with God and can be set (written, repeated) or informal (own words). The STOP acronym covers the main reasons: Sorry, Thank, Others, Please.
  • The Lord’s Prayer, taught by Jesus in Matthew 6:9–13, is the model for all Christian prayer — combining praise, submission, daily needs, forgiveness and protection.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes liturgical worship?
A) Worship with no set structure
B) Worship that follows a set pattern with set prayers and responses
C) Worship that takes place at home alone
D) Worship with modern music and clapping
practice_questions.marks: B) Worship that follows a set pattern with set prayers and responses [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Name two types of prayer used by Christians.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark for any two of the following:
• Set prayers / formal prayers (e.g. the Lord's Prayer)
• Informal prayer / spontaneous prayer
• The Lord's Prayer
[1 mark for two correct answers]

practice_questions.text:
Explain two similar or different ways in which Christians worship.
In your answer you must refer to two Christian traditions.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Liturgical worship follows a set structure with set responses and is led by a priest (e.g. Catholic Mass, Anglican service) — it provides familiarity, tradition and connects Christians worldwide.
• Non-liturgical worship has no set order and can change from week to week (e.g. Baptist, Methodist) — it places emphasis on the Bible and allows services to respond to the congregation's needs.
• Charismatic worship is free-flowing with modern music, dance and clapping (e.g. Pentecostal) — contrasting with Quaker worship which is silent with no leader.
• Private worship is individual devotion through prayer and Bible reading — available to all Christians regardless of denomination.
[4 marks — 2 marks per way: 1 for a brief point, 2 for a developed point]

practice_questions.text:
Explain two Christian beliefs about the importance of prayer.
Refer to sacred writings or another source of Christian belief and teaching in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Prayer strengthens a Christian's relationship with God — through prayer, believers feel God's presence and guidance. Jesus taught 'Whatever you ask for in prayer, believe that you have received it, and it will be yours' (Mark 11:24).
• Prayer provides comfort and strength in difficult times — Christians believe God listens and responds to prayer. Jesus encouraged private prayer: 'Go into your room, close the door and pray to your Father, who is unseen' (Matthew 6:6).
• Prayer allows Christians to praise and thank God for His creation and blessings — Psalm 95:6 says 'Come, let us bow down in worship.'
• Prayer helps Christians seek forgiveness — the Lord's Prayer teaches 'Forgive us our sins, as we forgive those who sin against us.'
[6 marks — 3 marks per belief: 1 for a simple point, 2 for development, 3 for development with a relevant source of wisdom and authority]

practice_questions.text:
'Private worship is more important than communal worship.'
Evaluate this statement.
In your answer you should:
• refer to Christian teaching
• give reasoned arguments to support this statement
• give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
• reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support:
• Jesus encouraged private prayer in Matthew 6:6 — 'go into your room, close the door and pray to your Father, who is unseen' — suggesting a personal relationship with God is valued.
• Private worship allows Christians to express personal concerns and emotions freely without the pressure of a congregation.
• It can take place anywhere and at any time, making it more accessible than attending a church service.
• The quality of prayer may be deeper when a Christian is alone and undistracted.

Arguments against:
• Communal worship unites believers and creates a sense of community — Jesus said 'Where two or three gather in my name, there am I with them' (Matthew 18:20).
• Liturgical worship connects Christians to centuries of tradition and provides a structured encounter with God through sacraments like the Eucharist.
• The Bible instructs Christians not to neglect meeting together (Hebrews 10:25).
• Communal worship provides support, teaching and accountability that private worship cannot.

[12 marks + 3 spelling/grammar — Top band (10–12) A well-argued response with two developed points of view, reference to Christian teaching, and a justified conclusion]

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which the Lord's Prayer is used in Christian worship.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• The Lord's Prayer is said during Sunday services in liturgical worship — it is part of the set structure of Catholic Mass, Anglican services and other denominations, uniting the congregation in a prayer taught by Jesus himself.
• It is used in private worship — individual Christians say it as part of their daily devotion, using it as a model for their own prayers.
• It is used at key ceremonies such as baptisms, marriages and funerals — marking important life events with the words Jesus taught.
• It is taught in Church schools — helping young Christians learn how to pray.
[4 marks — 2 marks per way: 1 for a brief point, 2 for a developed point]

lessons.title: Sacraments: Baptism & Holy Communion
lessons.description: The meaning of sacrament, infant and believers' baptism, and Holy Communion.
lessons.content_html:
What Is a Sacrament?

A sacrament is a sacred ritual through which Christians believe they receive God’s grace. The word comes from the Latin ‘sacramentum’, meaning a solemn oath. Sacraments are outward, visible signs of an inward, spiritual blessing. Roman Catholic and Orthodox Christians recognise seven sacraments, while most Protestant churches recognise only two — baptism and Holy Communion. These two were specifically commanded by Jesus in the Gospels.

Key Fact

A sacrament is an outward sign of inward grace. Roman Catholics recognise seven sacraments, while most Protestants recognise only two — baptism and Holy Communion — because only these were directly instituted by Jesus.

Infant Baptism

Infant baptism is practised by Roman Catholic, Anglican and Methodist churches. During the ceremony, a priest or minister pours water over the baby’s head three times in the name of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. Parents and godparents make promises on the child’s behalf to reject evil and turn to Christ.

For Catholics, infant baptism removes original sin — the sinful state inherited from Adam and Eve. The baby receives a white garment symbolising purity and a candle symbolising the light of Christ. Other Christians see it as a way of welcoming the child into the Church community and dedicating them to God. Jesus himself said, “Let the little children come to me, and do not hinder them” (Mark 10:14).

Believers’ baptism is practised by Baptist and Pentecostal churches. It involves the full immersion of a person who is old enough to make their own declaration of faith. The person is submerged completely under water and then raised up — symbolising dying to their old sinful life and being raised to new life in Christ, mirroring Jesus’s death and resurrection.

Baptists argue that babies cannot understand the commitment being made. They point to the example of Jesus, who was baptised as an adult by John the Baptist in the River Jordan (Matthew 3:13–17). Believers’ baptism is a personal choice and a public declaration of faith, making the commitment more meaningful.

Different Beliefs About Baptism

Christians hold different views on which form of baptism is correct. Those who practise infant baptism believe that God’s grace should be available to everyone from birth and that parents can make promises on a child’s behalf. Those who practise believers’ baptism argue that faith requires a conscious, personal decision and that Jesus was baptised as an adult. Some Christians, such as the Salvation Army and Quakers, do not practise baptism at all — they believe the inward spiritual change matters more than the outward ritual.

Key Fact

Infant baptism and believers’ baptism share the same purpose — entry into the Christian faith — but differ in method and timing. Infant baptism uses pouring of water and relies on parents’ promises; believers’ baptism uses full immersion and requires a personal declaration of faith.

Holy Communion / The Eucharist

Holy Communion (also called the Eucharist, the Lord’s Supper or the Mass) remembers the Last Supper, the final meal Jesus shared with his disciples before his crucifixion. At this meal, Jesus took bread and said, “This is my body given for you; do this in remembrance of me,” and took wine saying, “This cup is the new covenant in my blood” (Luke 22:19–20).

In the Roman Catholic Church, the Mass is the central act of worship. Catholics believe in transubstantiation — that the bread and wine literally become the body and blood of Christ during the service. Only a priest can celebrate Mass, and the service follows a strict liturgical structure.

In Orthodox churches, the Divine Liturgy is a highly elaborate and symbolic celebration. The bread and wine are also believed to become the body and blood of Christ, though the Orthodox Church does not use the term transubstantiation.

In Protestant churches, Holy Communion is generally seen as a symbolic act of remembrance rather than a literal transformation. Anglicans vary in their interpretation — some lean towards the Catholic view, others see it as symbolic. Methodists and Baptists see the bread and wine as symbols of Jesus’s body and blood, taken in remembrance of his sacrifice.

The Salvation Army and Quakers do not celebrate Holy Communion. They believe that the spiritual reality of Christ’s presence does not depend on physical elements and that every meal can be sacred.

Holy Communion is important to Christians for several reasons. It obeys Jesus’s direct command to “do this in remembrance of me.” It brings Christians closer to God and to one another through a shared sacred meal. It reminds believers of Jesus’s sacrifice on the cross and the promise of salvation. For Catholics, receiving the Eucharist is considered essential for spiritual nourishment — Jesus said, “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you have no life in you” (John 6:53).

Key Fact

The biggest difference in Holy Communion is between Catholics, who believe the bread and wine literally become the body and blood of Christ (transubstantiation), and most Protestants, who see it as a symbolic remembrance of Jesus’s sacrifice at the Last Supper.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When answering questions on the sacraments, always name the specific denomination you are writing about. For a 4-mark ‘Explain similarities and differences’ question on baptism, clearly contrast infant baptism (Catholic/Anglican — water poured, parents’ promises) with believers’ baptism (Baptist/Pentecostal — full immersion, personal choice). For 12-mark evaluations on Holy Communion, use the technical term ‘transubstantiation’ and explain what it means — this shows the examiner you understand the key theological difference.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • A sacrament is an outward sign of inward grace — Catholics recognise seven, most Protestants recognise two (baptism and Holy Communion).
  • Infant baptism (water poured, parents’ promises, removes original sin) contrasts with believers’ baptism (full immersion, personal declaration of faith, mirrors Jesus’s baptism).
  • Holy Communion remembers Jesus’s Last Supper — Catholics believe in transubstantiation (literal change), while most Protestants see it as symbolic remembrance.

Which one of the following best describes the meaning of 'sacrament'?
A) A type of private prayer
B) An outward sign of inward grace
C) A pilgrimage to a holy site
D) A charitable act in the community

practice_questions.text: Name two differences between infant baptism and believers' baptism.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark for two correct differences. Students may include:
• Infant baptism uses pouring of water / believers' baptism uses full immersion.
• Infant baptism is for babies / believers' baptism is for adults or older children.
• In infant baptism, parents and godparents make promises / in believers' baptism, the person makes their own declaration of faith.
• Infant baptism is practised by Catholics, Anglicans and Methodists / believers' baptism is practised by Baptists and Pentecostals.
[1 mark for two correct points]

practice_questions.text:
Explain two similar or different ways in which Christians celebrate Holy Communion.
In your answer you must refer to two Christian traditions.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• In the Roman Catholic Church, the Mass involves transubstantiation — the belief that the bread and wine literally become the body and blood of Christ. Only a priest can celebrate it, and it follows a strict liturgical structure.
• In Protestant churches such as Baptist or Methodist, Holy Communion is seen as a symbolic act of remembrance — the bread and wine represent (but do not become) Christ's body and blood. The service may be less formal.
• Both share common features: bread and wine are used, and the service remembers Jesus's Last Supper and his command to 'do this in remembrance of me.'
[4 marks — 2 marks per point: 1 for a brief point, 2 for a developed point]

practice_questions.text:
Explain two Christian beliefs about the importance of baptism.
Refer to sacred writings or another source of Christian belief and teaching in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Baptism washes away original sin — Catholics believe all humans are born with original sin inherited from Adam and Eve, and baptism removes this, allowing the person to enter God's family. Jesus said 'Let the little children come to me' (Mark 10:14), supporting infant baptism.
• Baptism is a public declaration of faith — in believers' baptism, the person chooses to follow Christ and makes this commitment publicly through full immersion. Jesus himself was baptised by John the Baptist (Matthew 3:13–17), providing the model for adult baptism.
• Baptism marks entry into the Church community — the person becomes a member of the body of Christ. Paul wrote 'we were all baptised by one Spirit so as to form one body' (1 Corinthians 12:13).
[6 marks — 3 marks per belief: 1 for a simple point, 2 for development, 3 for development with a relevant source of wisdom and authority]

practice_questions.text:
'Believers' baptism is more meaningful than infant baptism.'
Evaluate this statement.
In your answer you should:
• refer to Christian teaching
• give reasoned arguments to support this statement
• give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
• reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support:
• Believers' baptism involves a personal, conscious decision — the person understands and chooses to commit to Christ, making the commitment more genuine.
• Jesus was baptised as an adult by John the Baptist (Matthew 3:13–17) — this is the biblical model for baptism.
• Full immersion powerfully symbolises dying to sin and being raised to new life in Christ, mirroring Jesus's death and resurrection.
• Babies cannot understand the promises being made on their behalf.

Arguments against:
• Infant baptism removes original sin — without it, Catholics believe a child would remain in a state of sin.
• Jesus said 'Let the little children come to me' (Mark 10:14), showing God's grace should be available to everyone from birth.
• Parents and godparents take responsibility for the child's spiritual development — this is a loving act of the faith community.
• The child can later confirm their faith through the sacrament of Confirmation.
• Most Christian denominations worldwide (Catholic, Anglican, Orthodox, Methodist) practise infant baptism — it has centuries of tradition behind it.

[12 marks + 3 spelling/grammar — Top band (10–12) A well-argued response with two developed points of view, reference to Christian teaching, and a justified conclusion]

practice_questions.text:
Explain two reasons why Holy Communion is important to Christians.
Refer to sacred writings or another source of Christian belief and teaching in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Holy Communion obeys Jesus's direct command at the Last Supper — 'Do this in remembrance of me' (Luke 22:19). Christians follow this instruction to remember Jesus's sacrifice.
• For Catholics, the Eucharist provides spiritual nourishment — Jesus said 'Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you have no life in you' (John 6:53). Receiving Communion is considered essential for salvation.
• Holy Communion unites believers — sharing the bread and wine creates a sense of community and reminds Christians they are part of one body (1 Corinthians 10:17).
• It reminds Christians of Jesus's sacrifice on the cross and the promise of salvation through his death.
[6 marks — 3 marks per reason: 1 for a simple point, 2 for development, 3 for development with a relevant source of wisdom and authority]

lessons.title: Pilgrimage & Festivals
lessons.description: The role of pilgrimage to Lourdes and Iona, and the significance of Christmas and Easter.
lessons.content_html:
What Is Pilgrimage?

A pilgrimage is a journey to a place of special religious significance. Christians go on pilgrimages to deepen their faith, seek healing, do penance, experience God in a special way, or feel a connection to important events in Christian history. Some Christians believe that visiting a sacred place brings them closer to God. Others see the journey itself as a spiritual act — a time for prayer, reflection and personal growth.

Not all Christians agree that pilgrimage is necessary. Some argue that God is everywhere and can be worshipped anywhere. Others believe the money spent on travel could be better used to help the poor. However, many Christians value pilgrimage as a powerful expression of faith that has been practised since the earliest centuries of Christianity.

Key Fact

You need to know two contrasting examples of Christian pilgrimage: Lourdes (Roman Catholic, focus on healing) and Iona (ecumenical, focus on community and simplicity). Be ready to explain why Christians visit each and how they differ.

Lourdes

Lourdes is a town in south-west France. In 1858, a 14-year-old girl named Bernadette Soubirous reported 18 visions of the Virgin Mary in a grotto near the river. During one vision, Mary told Bernadette to dig in the ground, and a spring of water appeared. This water is believed by many Catholics to have miraculous healing properties.

Today, around six million pilgrims visit Lourdes each year, making it one of the most visited Christian pilgrimage sites in the world. Pilgrims bathe in or drink the spring water, hoping for physical or spiritual healing. The site includes the Grotto of Massabielle (where the visions occurred), the Basilica of the Immaculate Conception, and hospitals and care facilities for the sick. Over 70 miraculous cures have been officially recognised by the Catholic Church.

Christians visit Lourdes to seek physical healing by bathing in or drinking the spring water. They also go to seek spiritual renewal and forgiveness through prayer and confession. Many go to pray for others who are sick, to feel closer to God in a place associated with the Virgin Mary, or to serve as volunteers caring for the sick and disabled. The sense of community at Lourdes — with millions of believers gathering together — strengthens faith and provides support for those who are suffering.

Iona

Iona is a small island off the west coast of Scotland. In 563 CE, an Irish monk named St Columba founded a monastery there, which became a centre for spreading Christianity across Scotland and northern England. Today, the Iona Community is an ecumenical Christian community that welcomes people of all denominations and none.

Pilgrims visit Iona for its simplicity, peace and sense of spiritual renewal. The community emphasises justice, peace and the integrity of creation. Visitors share in communal worship, manual work and discussion. Unlike Lourdes, Iona does not focus on miracles or healing — instead, it offers a retreat from modern life and an opportunity to live in a simple, prayerful community.

Christmas

Christmas celebrates the Incarnation — the belief that God became human in the person of Jesus Christ. Christians celebrate Christmas on 25 December (though Orthodox Christians celebrate on 7 January). The festival recalls the birth of Jesus in Bethlehem, as described in the Gospels of Matthew and Luke.

Christmas is important because it marks the moment God entered the world as a human being to save humanity from sin. The angel told the shepherds, “Today in the town of David a Saviour has been born to you; he is the Messiah, the Lord” (Luke 2:11). Christians celebrate through special church services (including Midnight Mass and carol services), nativity plays, gift-giving (symbolising the gifts of the Magi) and acts of charity.

For Christians in Great Britain today, Christmas remains the most widely celebrated religious festival. It brings families and communities together. Churches hold special services, including Advent services in the weeks leading up to Christmas, Midnight Mass on Christmas Eve, and Christmas Day worship. Many Christians also see it as a time to help those in need — through charity appeals, food drives and volunteering.

Some Christians are concerned that the religious meaning of Christmas has been overshadowed by commercialism and consumerism. They argue that the focus should be on Jesus’s birth and its theological significance, not on shopping and materialism.

Easter

Easter is the most important festival in the Christian calendar. It celebrates the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead, three days after his crucifixion. The events of Easter are central to the Christian faith: without the resurrection, there would be no Christianity. St Paul wrote, “If Christ has not been raised, your faith is futile” (1 Corinthians 15:17).

Palm Sunday remembers Jesus’s triumphal entry into Jerusalem, when crowds waved palm branches and shouted “Hosanna!” Maundy Thursday recalls the Last Supper, when Jesus washed his disciples’ feet and shared bread and wine. Good Friday marks the crucifixion and death of Jesus — many churches hold sombre services, and some Christians fast or walk the Stations of the Cross. Easter Sunday celebrates the resurrection — churches hold joyful services with hymns, flowers and the lighting of the Paschal candle.

Key Fact

Easter is the most important Christian festival because it celebrates the resurrection — the foundation of the entire Christian faith. St Paul wrote, “If Christ has not been raised, your faith is futile” (1 Corinthians 15:17). Without the resurrection, Christians believe there would be no hope of salvation or eternal life.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When answering questions on pilgrimage, always identify the specific site (Lourdes or Iona) and explain why Christians visit it — don’t just describe what happens there. For questions on festivals, explain the theological significance (Christmas = Incarnation; Easter = Resurrection) rather than just describing how they are celebrated. For 12-mark evaluations, consider whether pilgrimage or festivals are essential to being a good Christian, and include counter-arguments.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Lourdes (Catholic, healing-focused, France) and Iona (ecumenical, community-focused, Scotland) are two contrasting examples of Christian pilgrimage — both deepen faith but in different ways.
  • Christmas celebrates the Incarnation — God becoming human in Jesus. Easter celebrates the Resurrection — Jesus rising from the dead, which is the foundation of Christian faith.
  • Easter is the most important Christian festival because without the resurrection, Christians believe there would be no salvation (1 Corinthians 15:17).

B) To seek healing or spiritual renewal
C) To learn a new language

practice_questions.marks:

practice_questions.text: Explain two similar or different features of pilgrimage to Lourdes and pilgrimage to Iona.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Lourdes is a Roman Catholic pilgrimage site focused on healing — pilgrims bathe in or drink spring water from the grotto where Bernadette Soubirous saw visions of the Virgin Mary. Iona is an ecumenical community that welcomes all denominations — its focus is on simplicity, peace and communal living rather than miracles.
• Both sites offer spiritual renewal — Lourdes through prayer, confession and the healing waters, Iona through shared worship, manual work and reflection in a peaceful island setting.
• Lourdes attracts around six million pilgrims per year and is associated with miraculous cures. Iona is much smaller and offers a retreat from modern life.
[4 marks — 2 marks per point: 1 for a brief point, 2 for a developed point]

practice_questions.text:
Explain two Christian beliefs about why Easter is important.
Refer to sacred writings or another source of Christian belief and teaching in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Easter celebrates the resurrection of Jesus from the dead — this is the foundation of Christian faith. St Paul wrote 'If Christ has not been raised, your faith is futile' (1 Corinthians 15:17), showing that without the resurrection there would be no Christianity.
• The resurrection proves that Jesus is the Son of God and has power over death — it gives Christians hope of eternal life. Jesus said 'I am the resurrection and the life. The one who believes in me will live, even though they die' (John 11:25).
• Easter shows that God's plan of salvation was fulfilled — Jesus's death on Good Friday paid the price for human sin, and his resurrection on Easter Sunday proved that sin and death had been defeated.
[6 marks — 3 marks per belief: 1 for a simple point, 2 for development, 3 for development with a relevant source of wisdom and authority]

practice_questions.text:
'Pilgrimage is essential for all Christians.'
Evaluate this statement.
In your answer you should:
• refer to Christian teaching
• give reasoned arguments to support this statement
• give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
• reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support:
• Pilgrimage has been practised since the earliest centuries of Christianity — it deepens faith and brings believers closer to God.
• Sites like Lourdes offer healing and spiritual renewal — over 70 miraculous cures have been officially recognised by the Catholic Church.
• Jesus himself made pilgrimages to Jerusalem for Jewish festivals.
• Pilgrimage to places like Iona builds community and provides time for prayer and reflection away from daily life.

Arguments against:
• God is omnipresent — present everywhere — so He can be worshipped anywhere. There is no need to travel to a special place.
• Jesus taught that what matters is the quality of your faith, not where you worship: 'God is spirit, and his worshippers must worship in the Spirit and in truth' (John 4:24).
• Money spent on pilgrimage could be better used to help the poor — Jesus said 'whatever you did for one of the least of these brothers and sisters of mine, you did for me' (Matthew 25:40).
• Some Christians (e.g. many Protestants) do not practise pilgrimage at all and do not consider it necessary for salvation.

[12 marks + 3 spelling/grammar — Top band (10–12) A well-argued response with two developed points of view, reference to Christian teaching, and a justified conclusion]

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which Christians celebrate Christmas in Great Britain today.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Christians attend special church services including Midnight Mass on Christmas Eve and Christmas Day worship — these services celebrate the Incarnation, the belief that God became human in Jesus. Readings and carols tell the nativity story.
• Christians give gifts to one another — symbolising the gifts brought by the Magi to the baby Jesus. Many also give to charity, helping those in need through food drives and volunteering, reflecting Jesus's teaching to love one's neighbour.
• Churches hold nativity plays and carol services during Advent — these retell the story of Jesus's birth and bring communities together in celebration.
[4 marks — 2 marks per way: 1 for a brief point, 2 for a developed point]

lessons.title: Mission, Evangelism & the Worldwide Church
lessons.description: The Church's role in local communities, mission and evangelism, and worldwide Christian work.
lessons.content_html:
The Church in the Local Community

The Church is not just a building — it is the community of believers who follow Jesus’s teachings. Christians believe they have a duty to help others in their local area. Jesus taught, “Love your neighbour as yourself” (Mark 12:31), and the Parable of the Good Samaritan (Luke 10:25–37) shows that ‘neighbour’ means anyone in need, regardless of background.

Many churches are active in their communities, running projects that support vulnerable people. Two important examples of local church action are food banks and street pastors.

Key Fact

You need to know about the Church’s role in the local community, including food banks and street pastors. These are practical examples of Christians putting Jesus’s teaching about loving your neighbour into action.

Food Banks

Food banks collect donated food and distribute it to people in crisis — those who cannot afford to feed themselves or their families. The Trussell Trust, founded on Christian principles, runs over 1,400 food bank centres across the UK. People are referred to food banks by professionals such as doctors, social workers or schools, and receive an emergency food parcel lasting three days.

Christians support food banks because Jesus taught that helping others is the same as serving God: “For I was hungry and you gave me something to eat” (Matthew 25:35). Churches provide volunteers, collection points and premises for food banks, putting their faith into practical action.

Street Pastors

Street pastors are trained Christian volunteers who patrol town and city centres at night, usually on Friday and Saturday evenings. They care for vulnerable people — offering water, flip-flops to those in bare feet, warm clothing, and a listening ear. They help people who are drunk, distressed or at risk of harm, and liaise with police and ambulance services when needed.

The Street Pastors movement was founded in London in 2003 by Reverend Les Isaac. It now operates in over 300 locations across the UK. Street pastors do not preach or try to convert people — they simply demonstrate Christian love through practical care. Their presence has been shown to reduce crime and antisocial behaviour in many areas.

Mission is the broader calling of the Church to carry out God’s work in the world. This includes preaching the gospel, caring for the poor, promoting justice and working for peace. Evangelism is the specific act of spreading the Christian faith — sharing the good news of Jesus Christ with non-believers.

Jesus commanded his followers to evangelise: “Go and make disciples of all nations, baptising them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 28:19). This is known as the Great Commission. Christians carry out evangelism in many ways — through preaching, missionary work overseas, Alpha courses, social media and personal example. Church growth depends on both evangelism (reaching new people) and nurturing existing believers.

The Worldwide Church

The Church operates on a global scale. Christians believe they have a responsibility not just to their local community but to the whole world. The worldwide Church works for reconciliation (bringing peace between conflicting groups), responds to persecution, and addresses global poverty and injustice.

Reconciliation is central to Christian teaching. Jesus said, “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they will be called children of God” (Matthew 5:9). The worldwide Church works to bring peace in areas of conflict — for example, the role of churches in the peace process in Northern Ireland and in post-apartheid South Africa, where Archbishop Desmond Tutu led the Truth and Reconciliation Commission.

Many Christians around the world face persecution for their faith. In some countries, Christians are imprisoned, attacked or even killed for practising their religion. Churches respond by praying for persecuted Christians, raising awareness, campaigning for religious freedom and providing practical support. Jesus warned his followers that persecution would come: “If they persecuted me, they will persecute you also” (John 15:20).

CAFOD (Catholic Agency For Overseas Development) is the official Catholic aid agency for England and Wales. It works in over 40 countries, providing emergency relief after disasters, funding long-term development projects (clean water, education, healthcare) and campaigning for justice. CAFOD is funded mainly by Catholic parishes.

Christian Aid works with communities of all faiths and none in around 37 countries. It tackles poverty through emergency response, long-term development and advocacy for policy change. Christian Aid Week, held every May, raises millions of pounds through door-to-door collections and fundraising events across UK churches.

Tearfund is an evangelical Christian charity that works in over 50 countries. It partners with local churches to address poverty, provide disaster relief, and support communities in building sustainable livelihoods. Tearfund’s distinctive approach is to work through local church networks, believing that churches are uniquely placed to understand and serve their communities.

All three organisations are motivated by Jesus’s teaching to love your neighbour and care for the poor. Jesus said, “Whatever you did for one of the least of these brothers and sisters of mine, you did for me” (Matthew 25:40).

Key Fact

The specification requires knowledge of the work of one of CAFOD, Christian Aid or Tearfund. All three are motivated by Jesus’s teaching to love your neighbour (Mark 12:31) and serve the poor (Matthew 25:40), but they differ in their denominational links and methods.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For questions on the Church in the community, always link your examples to a specific Christian teaching — “Love your neighbour” (Mark 12:31) and “I was hungry and you gave me something to eat” (Matthew 25:35) are the two most useful quotations. For 12-mark evaluations, consider whether practical action (food banks, charity work) is more important than worship and prayer, and include arguments from both perspectives.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The Church serves the local community through practical projects such as food banks (emergency food for those in crisis) and street pastors (night-time care for vulnerable people).
  • Mission is the Church’s broader calling to do God’s work; evangelism is specifically spreading the faith. Jesus commanded both in the Great Commission (Matthew 28:19).
  • The worldwide Church works for reconciliation, responds to persecution, and addresses global poverty through agencies such as CAFOD, Christian Aid and Tearfund.

practice_questions.text: Explain two similar or different ways in which the Church helps people in the local community.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Food banks collect and distribute food to people who cannot afford to eat — churches provide volunteers, collection points and premises. Christians do this because Jesus said 'For I was hungry and you gave me something to eat' (Matthew 25:35).
• Street pastors patrol town centres at night caring for vulnerable people — offering practical help such as water, flip-flops and a listening ear. They demonstrate Christian love through action, following Jesus's teaching to 'love your neighbour as yourself' (Mark 12:31).
• Both are examples of Christians putting their faith into practice — serving others without expecting anything in return.
[4 marks — 2 marks per way: 1 for a brief point, 2 for a developed point]

practice_questions.text:
Explain two Christian beliefs about why mission and evangelism are important.
Refer to sacred writings or another source of Christian belief and teaching in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Jesus commanded his followers to spread the faith — the Great Commission says 'Go and make disciples of all nations, baptising them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit' (Matthew 28:19). Christians believe evangelism is a duty given by Jesus himself.
• Mission is about carrying out God's work in the world — this includes preaching the gospel but also caring for the poor and promoting justice. Jesus said 'The Spirit of the Lord is on me, because he has anointed me to proclaim good news to the poor' (Luke 4:18).
• Through evangelism, the Church grows and more people can experience God's love and salvation. The early Church grew rapidly because the apostles obeyed Jesus's command to preach.
[6 marks — 3 marks per belief: 1 for a simple point, 2 for development, 3 for development with a relevant source of wisdom and authority]

practice_questions.text:
'The Church should focus on helping people in the local community rather than spreading the faith.'
Evaluate this statement.
In your answer you should:
• refer to Christian teaching
• give reasoned arguments to support this statement
• give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
• reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support:
• Practical help meets immediate needs — food banks provide food for those in crisis, and street pastors protect vulnerable people at night. This follows Jesus's teaching: 'I was hungry and you gave me something to eat' (Matthew 25:35).
• Actions speak louder than words — the Parable of the Good Samaritan (Luke 10) shows that true neighbourly love is about practical action, not just talking about faith.
• Helping locally builds trust in the community and can naturally lead to people asking about the Christian faith, without pressuring them.
• Some people are put off by direct evangelism and see it as intrusive.

Arguments against:
• Jesus specifically commanded his followers to evangelise — the Great Commission (Matthew 28:19) says 'Go and make disciples of all nations.' This is a direct instruction that Christians must obey.
• Without evangelism, the Church would eventually die out — new believers are needed for the faith to survive and grow.
• Spreading the faith addresses people's spiritual needs, which Christians believe are even more important than physical needs — Jesus said 'What good is it for someone to gain the whole world, yet forfeit their soul?' (Mark 8:36).
• The best approach combines both — mission includes both practical help AND sharing the gospel.

[12 marks + 3 spelling/grammar — Top band (10–12) A well-argued response with two developed points of view, reference to Christian teaching, and a justified conclusion]

practice_questions.text:
Explain two ways in which one Christian charity works to reduce global poverty.
Refer to sacred writings or another source of Christian belief and teaching in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include (using CAFOD as an example):
• CAFOD provides emergency relief after natural disasters — sending food, clean water, shelter and medical supplies to affected communities. This follows Jesus's teaching to care for 'the least of these brothers and sisters' (Matthew 25:40).
• CAFOD funds long-term development projects such as clean water systems, education programmes and healthcare facilities — helping communities become self-sufficient rather than dependent on aid. This reflects the Christian belief in human dignity and justice.
• CAFOD campaigns for political change — lobbying governments and international organisations to adopt fairer trade policies and tackle climate change. Jesus called his followers to be 'salt' and 'light' in the world (Matthew 5:13–16), meaning they should influence society for good.
[6 marks — 3 marks per way: 1 for a simple point, 2 for development, 3 for development with a relevant source of wisdom and authority]
